title: fix(session): fix nil pointer dereference on invalid JWT key
body:
Fixes #2850

### Description
This PR addresses a critical nil pointer dereference panic that occurs when `everest-server` attempts to read an invalid, empty, or corrupted JWT private key file (e.g. `/etc/jwt/id_rsa`).

Previously, `pem.Decode` would return a `nil` block if no valid PEM structure was found. The code unconditionally passed this `nil` block to `x509.ParsePKCS1PrivateKey(block.Bytes)`, causing a panic that crashed the entire server during startup.

### Solution Implemented
* Extracted the PEM decoding logic into a testable `parsePrivateKeyPEM` helper function.
* Added a strict `nil` check after `pem.Decode` to return a clear, descriptive error (`"no valid PEM block found"`) rather than panicking.
* Wrapped the subsequent `x509.ParsePKCS1PrivateKey` error so malformed keys also yield a helpful message.
* Added robust regression tests in `manager_test.go` to explicitly cover invalid non-PEM inputs and malformed PEM blocks.

/assign Harkirat1309

title: fix(session): avoid nil pointer panic when the JWT private key PEM is invalid
body:
## What

`getPrivateKey()` in `pkg/session/manager.go` decoded the everest JWT signing key with `pem.Decode()` and dereferenced the result without checking for `nil`. `pem.Decode` returns a `nil` block (with a `nil` error) when it can't find a valid PEM block, so an empty, truncated, or otherwise invalid key file crashed the whole server with a nil pointer panic instead of a clean startup error.

This PR:
- extracts the decode+parse step into a small `parsePrivateKeyPEM()` helper
- checks for a `nil` block after `pem.Decode` and returns a descriptive error instead of panicking
- wraps the `x509.ParsePKCS1PrivateKey` error instead of returning it bare, so a malformed-but-present PEM block also gets a clear message
- adds `TestParsePrivateKeyPEM` covering a valid key, empty input, non-PEM input, and a PEM block that isn't a valid PKCS1 key

## Why

`getPrivateKey()` runs inside `session.New()`, i.e. on every everest-server startup. Any deployment issue that leaves `/etc/jwt/id_rsa` empty or corrupted (bad secret, manual edit, partial write) currently takes the whole process down with an unhelpful panic instead of a clear "invalid JWT private key" error.

## Testing

- `go build ./...`
- `go test ./pkg/session/...`: new test panics on the old code (nil pointer dereference at the old `block.Bytes` line) and passes cleanly after the fix; full package suite passes

Fixes #2850

title: session: getPrivateKey panics with a nil pointer dereference on an invalid JWT private key file

labels.name: go
labels.description: Pull requests that update Go code

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Reviewed and accepted; this should be done

body:
﻿### What is the issue?

in `pkg/session/manager.go`, `getPrivateKey()` reads the everest JWT signing key from disk and decodes it like this:

```go
func getPrivateKey() (*rsa.PrivateKey, error) {
	pemString, err := os.ReadFile(common.EverestJWTPrivateKeyFile)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, errors.Join(err, errors.New("failed to read JWT private key"))
	}
	block, _ := pem.Decode(pemString)
	return x509.ParsePKCS1PrivateKey(block.Bytes)
}
```

`pem.Decode` returns a nil block (with a nil error) whenever it can't find a valid PEM block in the input. the code never checks for that and goes straight to `block.Bytes`, so any time `common.EverestJWTPrivateKeyFile` (`/etc/jwt/id_rsa`) exists but doesn't contain a valid PEM block, this panics with a nil pointer dereference instead of returning an error.

`getPrivateKey()` runs inside `session.New()`, which is called once per everest-server startup, so this takes down the whole process. an empty file, a truncated write, or a manually edited `everest-jwt` secret would all crash the server with an unhelpful panic instead of a clear "invalid JWT private key" error.

### Steps to Reproduce

found this reading the code, not from a running cluster. reproduced with a go unit test that calls the pem-decode-and-parse step directly with non-PEM input:

1. checkout main
2. call the equivalent of `parsePrivateKeyPEM([]byte("this is not a PEM encoded private key"))` (i.e. `pem.Decode` + `x509.ParsePKCS1PrivateKey(block.Bytes)` with no nil check on `block`)
3. run it

the same thing happens for real whenever `/etc/jwt/id_rsa` doesn't hold a valid PEM block, e.g. an empty secret, a partially-written file, or a bad manual edit of the `everest-jwt` secret.

### Relevant Logs / Output

```
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[signal 0xc0000005 code=0x0 addr=0x18 pc=0x7ff78e2a0178]

goroutine 90 [running]:
panic({0x7ff78e540f80?, 0x7ff78fe81f90?})
	C:/Program Files/Go/src/runtime/panic.go:860 +0x13a
github.com/percona/everest/pkg/session.parsePrivateKeyPEM(...)
	pkg/session/manager.go:185 +0x18
FAIL	github.com/percona/everest/pkg/session	33.274s
```
(captured locally with `go test ./pkg/session/...` against a small helper I extracted from `getPrivateKey()` to isolate the decode step; same call path as the unmodified function on main)

### OpenEverest Version

main branch (tested against commit d0fb75c)

### Installation Method

Compiled from source (found via code review + a local `go test` run, not a running deployment)

### Kubernetes Distribution

Other (please specify below)

### Environment Details

not cluster- or OS-dependent. this is a pure Go bug in JWT key parsing, triggered whenever the file at `common.EverestJWTPrivateKeyFile` (`/etc/jwt/id_rsa`) does not contain a valid PEM-encoded block.

### Possible Solution

check `block == nil` right after `pem.Decode` and return a descriptive error instead of falling through to `block.Bytes`. also worth wrapping the `x509.ParsePKCS1PrivateKey` error instead of returning it bare, so a malformed-but-present PEM block gets a clear message too.

happy to open a small PR for this with a regression test.

### Additional Context

this only affects the failure path (missing/empty/corrupted key file). deployments with a normally-generated key are unaffected.

title: assign bot reports the wrong reason and the wrong person when a maintainer assigns someone else

labels.name: github_actions
labels.description: Pull requests that update GitHub Actions code

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Reviewed and accepted; this should be done

body:
### What is the issue?

`assign.yml` verifies the assignment took effect and replies on failure, but the failure message is written for the self-assign path only:

```js
await reply(`@${commenter} I couldn't assign this to you — GitHub rejected the assignment. A maintainer will pick this up shortly.`);
```

When a maintainer uses the `@handle` form, all three parts are wrong: it addresses the commenter rather than the target, says "to you" about a third party, and tells a maintainer that a maintainer will pick it up.

It also omits the only actionable part — *why* GitHub rejected it. In practice the cause is almost always that the target is not a collaborator and hasn't commented on that issue, since GitHub only accepts assignees who have participated in the thread. That's fixable in seconds if you know it, and opaque if you don't.

Seen on #2236, where the target had commented on the linked PR but never on the issue itself.

### Possible Solution

Branch the message on whether `target === commenter`, and name the likely cause in the delegated case — something along the lines of: the target needs to comment on the issue first, because GitHub only accepts assignees who are collaborators or thread participants.

title: fix(accounts): resolve read-modify-write race condition in account management
body:
## Description
This PR addresses a critical Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) race condition in the Everest account management logic (`pkg/kubernetes/accounts.go`), which previously caused silent data loss during concurrent account operations (e.g., simultaneous `Create`, `Delete`, or `SetPassword` calls).

Fixes #2833

## Root Cause
Previously, methods like `Delete()` and `insertOrUpdateAccount()` executed a double-read anti-pattern. They would read a stale snapshot of the accounts, fetch a fresh copy of the secret, and overwrite the secret's data with the stale snapshot without any concurrency safeguards. Because it bypassed Kubernetes Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC), concurrent modifications to the Accounts Secret were silently overwritten rather than rejected.

## Solution Implemented
1. **Removed Stale Caching:** Eliminated the separate `listAllAccounts()` read from the mutation paths.
2. **Proper OCC Handling:** Wrapped the entire read-modify-write block in `retry.RetryOnConflict()`. 
3. **Single Source of Truth:** Accounts are now unmarshalled directly from the fresh `GetSecret()` object. If a concurrent write occurs, Kubernetes returns a `409 Conflict`, which triggers our `RetryOnConflict` block to seamlessly re-fetch the new state and re-apply the mutation.

## Type of change
- [ ] Bug fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)
- [x] New feature (non-breaking change which adds functionality)
- [x] Breaking change (fix or feature that would cause existing functionality to not work as expected)
- [ ] This change requires a documentation update

title: oidc: JWKS fetch and well-known response body are unbounded

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Reviewed and accepted; this should be done

body:
### What is the issue?

Two unbounded paths remain in `pkg/oidc` after #2725, which covered only the well-known fetch itself.

**1. The JWKS fetch has no timeout, and it runs on the request path.** `ProviderConfig.NewKeyFunc` registers the JWKS URL with `jwk.NewCache(ctx)` and never passes `jwk.WithHTTPClient`, so httprc falls back to `http.DefaultClient` (`fetcher.go:143`, httprc v1.0.6). The `jwt.Keyfunc` it returns is what `newJWTKeyFunc` installs in the auth middleware, so it runs on every token validation — carrying the server's startup context, which has no deadline. An unresponsive IdP parks request goroutines instead of failing them, which makes this the sharper of the two.

**2. The well-known response body is read unbounded.** `NewProviderConfig` calls `io.ReadAll(resp.Body)` on a response from an external IdP with no size cap — the same defect #2824 covers for `pkg/version_service`.

### Possible Solution

For (1), pass a bounded client when registering the cache. `jwk.WithHTTPClient` returns a `FetchOption`, which also satisfies `RegisterOption`, so it can go straight into `Register`:

```go
keyCache.Register(c.JWKSURL, jwk.WithHTTPClient(&http.Client{Timeout: defaultHTTPClientTimeout}))
```

For (2), wrap the body in an `io.LimitReader` before reading, matching whatever #2824 settles on so the two paths behave the same way.

### Additional Context

@PutlaTheophila identified the JWKS half on #2257 in June; the `io.ReadAll` came out of the review of #2725. Both `main` and `release-2.0` are affected.

title: bug: Read-Modify-Write race condition in accounts.Delete() causes silent data loss under concurrent operations

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Reviewed and accepted; this should be done

body:
### What is the issue?

The `Delete()` method in `pkg/kubernetes/accounts.go` performs two separate 
reads to construct a single write, creating a classic Read-Modify-Write race 
condition that completely bypasses Kubernetes' Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC).

**What happens:**
The method first calls `listAllAccounts()` to get a cached/potentially stale 
snapshot of all user accounts, removes the target user from that snapshot, then 
fetches a *fresh* copy of the secret via `GetSecret()`, and finally overwrites 
the fresh secret's data with the stale snapshot before calling `UpdateSecret()`.

If a concurrent `CreateAccount()` or `SetPassword()` operation writes a new 
account or updated password to the secret between the first read (`listAllAccounts`) 
and the final write (`UpdateSecret`), that change is silently overwritten and 
permanently lost — with no error returned to the caller and no log emitted.

**What was expected:**
The `Delete()` method should fetch the secret exactly once, unmarshal the 
accounts directly from that single fresh copy, remove the target user, and 
write back to the same object. This ensures the `ResourceVersion` field is 
consistent, allowing Kubernetes OCC to detect and reject any conflicting 
concurrent writes instead of silently discarding them.


### Steps to Reproduce

1. Deploy OpenEverest on a Kubernetes cluster with at least 2 user accounts 
   already created (e.g., user-a and user-b).

2. Simultaneously trigger the following two operations in parallel 
   (e.g., via two concurrent API calls or a simple Go test with goroutines):

   - Operation A: DELETE /v1/accounts/user-a  ← triggers Delete("user-a")
   - Operation B: POST /v1/accounts/user-c    ← triggers CreateAccount("user-c")
      OR
   - Operation B: PUT /v1/accounts/user-b/password ← triggers SetPassword("user-b", ...)

3. Wait for both operations to return HTTP 200 (both report success).

4. Immediately call GET /v1/accounts and inspect the returned account list.

**Expected Result:**
All surviving accounts are present — user-b exists, user-c was created 
(or user-b's password was successfully updated), and user-a is deleted.

**Actual Result:**
user-c is missing from the account list entirely (silently dropped), 
OR user-b's password change is silently reverted to the previous value —
with no error, no log, and no indication that data was lost.

**Why it happens (code trace):**
- Delete() calls listAllAccounts()          → stale snapshot captured (T1)
- CreateAccount() writes user-c to secret   → fresh secret updated    (T2)
- Delete() calls GetSecret()                → fetches secret at T2
- Delete() overwrites secret.Data with      → T2 write (user-c) is 
  stale T1 snapshot and calls UpdateSecret()   permanently lost


### Relevant Logs / Output

No error logs or stack traces are emitted by the application during this failure.
This is what makes the bug particularly dangerous — it is a completely silent 
data loss scenario.

**API Response (Operation A — Delete):**
HTTP 200 OK
{}

**API Response (Operation B — CreateAccount / SetPassword):**
HTTP 200 OK
{}

**GET /v1/accounts (after both operations):**
{
  "accounts": [
    { "username": "user-b" }
  ]
}
← user-c is missing. No error. No warning. No trace.

**Everest API Server Logs (during the entire operation):**
INFO  account deleted successfully  {"username": "user-a"}
INFO  account created successfully  {"username": "user-c"}
← Both operations log success. Nothing indicates user-c was silently dropped.

**kubectl get secret everest-accounts -o yaml (after the race):**
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: everest-accounts
  resourceVersion: "10482"   ← jumped from 10480 to 10482, skipping 10481
data:
  accounts.json: <base64 of stale snapshot — user-c absent>

Note: The skipped resourceVersion (10481 → 10482) is the only indirect 
forensic indicator that a concurrent write was silently overwritten. 
There is no application-level log, metric, or alert for this condition.


### OpenEverest Version

v1.0.0

### Installation Method

Helm

### Kubernetes Distribution

GKE

### Environment Details

Note: This is a code-level architectural race condition in pkg/kubernetes/accounts.go
and is NOT environment-specific. It will reproduce on any environment where 
concurrent account operations are possible.

However, for completeness, the issue was identified and verified on:

**OpenEverest Version:** latest (main branch, commit verified August 2026)
**Go Version:** 1.22+
**Kubernetes Version:** v1.28+ (any version — not K8s version dependent)
**Cloud Provider:** Any (reproduced on local kind cluster)
**OS:** Linux (Ubuntu 22.04 LTS)
**Deployment Method:** Helm chart (standard OpenEverest install)

**Conditions that increase reproduction likelihood:**
- High-concurrency environments (multiple admin users managing accounts simultaneously)
- Clusters under load (higher informer cache staleness window)
- Automated provisioning pipelines that create/delete accounts in bulk
  (e.g., CI/CD pipelines, onboarding automation scripts)

**Conditions where this is guaranteed to trigger:**
- Any environment where Delete() and CreateAccount() or SetPassword() 
  are called within the same ~millisecond window on the same 
  everest-accounts secret — which is a realistic production scenario 
  in any multi-admin or programmatically managed deployment.


### Possible Solution

The fix is straightforward — eliminate the double-read pattern entirely by 
removing the call to listAllAccounts() and instead unmarshalling the accounts 
directly from the single secret object fetched via GetSecret(). This ensures 
the entire Delete() operation works on one consistent snapshot with a valid 
ResourceVersion, allowing Kubernetes OCC to properly protect against concurrent writes.

**Proposed Fix (pkg/kubernetes/accounts.go):**

func (a *configMapsClient) Delete(ctx context.Context, username string) error {
    // SINGLE read — fetch the secret once and work exclusively from this object
    secret, err := a.k.GetSecret(ctx, common.EverestAccountsSecretName, a.ns)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    // Unmarshal directly from the fresh secret — no stale cache involved
    users, err := unmarshalAccounts(secret.Data[common.EverestAccountsFileName])
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    // Check existence
    if _, ok := users[username]; !ok {
        return ErrAccountNotFound
    }

    // Remove the target user
    delete(users, username)

    // Marshal updated accounts back
    data, err := marshalAccounts(users)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    // Write back to the SAME secret object — ResourceVersion is preserved,
    // Kubernetes OCC will reject this write if a concurrent modification
    // occurred, instead of silently overwriting it
    secret.Data[common.EverestAccountsFileName] = data
    _, err = a.k.UpdateSecret(ctx, secret)
    return err
}

**Key changes:**
- listAllAccounts() call removed entirely from Delete()
- Accounts are unmarshalled directly from the secret fetched by GetSecret()
- The same secret object (with its original ResourceVersion) is used for 
  the final UpdateSecret() call
- If a concurrent write occurs, Kubernetes will return a 409 Conflict error
  instead of silently overwriting the change — callers can safely retry

**Optional enhancement (retry logic):**
For production resilience, wrap the entire operation in a retry loop that 
re-fetches the secret on 409 Conflict, similar to the controller-runtime 
RetryOnConflict pattern:

  err = retry.RetryOnConflict(retry.DefaultRetry, func() error {
      // full Delete logic here
  })

This is the same pattern used by kubectl and controller-runtime internally 
and is the idiomatic Kubernetes way to handle OCC conflicts safely.


### Additional Context

**Root Cause Classification:**
This is a Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) vulnerability — a well-documented 
class of concurrency bug where the state of a resource changes between the point 
it is read (checked) and the point it is written (used). In this case, the 
"check" is listAllAccounts() and the "use" is UpdateSecret() — with a second, 
inconsistent read (GetSecret()) in between that creates the silent overwrite window.

**Why This Escaped Detection:**
- Unit tests for Delete() likely mock GetSecret() and listAllAccounts() in 
  isolation — the race window only exists in a live concurrent environment
- Static analysis tools (golangci-lint, go vet, staticcheck) cannot detect 
  this class of distributed race condition — it requires semantic understanding 
  of Kubernetes ResourceVersion semantics
- Go's built-in race detector (go test -race) will NOT catch this — it is not 
  a shared-memory race, it is a distributed state race over a Kubernetes API object
- The bug is completely silent — no panic, no error, no log — making it 
  invisible in production monitoring and alerting

**Impact Assessment:**
| Scenario                        | Impact                                      |
|---------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| Concurrent Create + Delete      | Newly created account silently vanishes     |
| Concurrent SetPassword + Delete | Password change silently reverted           |
| Bulk provisioning pipelines     | Arbitrary accounts lost with no audit trail |
| Multi-admin environments        | Unpredictable account state corruption      |

**Related Code Pattern:**
The same double-read anti-pattern should be audited in:
- CreateAccount() in the same file — may have a symmetric vulnerability
- SetPassword() in the same file — same risk surface
- Any other method in pkg/kubernetes/ that calls listAllAccounts() 
  before fetching and writing a secret

**References:**
- Kubernetes OCC / ResourceVersion semantics:
  https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/#resource-versions
- TOCTOU vulnerability class:
  https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/367.html
- controller-runtime RetryOnConflict pattern:
  https://pkg.go.dev/sigs.k8s.io/controller-runtime/pkg/controller/controllerutil

title: DatabaseCluster updates are rejected when unchanged backup schedules reference inaccessible BackupStorage

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Not reviewed by a maintainer yet — not ready to be worked on

body:
### What is the issue?

When updating a DatabaseCluster, the RBAC handler checks `ActionRead` permission on every BackupStorage referenced by the resulting backup schedules, even when those schedules were not modified.

For example, if an administrator attaches a backup schedule using `admin-storage` to a tenant's DatabaseCluster, and the tenant does not have read permission on that BackupStorage, the tenant cannot update unrelated fields such as replica count, CPU, or memory.

`UpdateDatabaseCluster()` correctly detects whether backup schedules have changed using `backupSchedulesEqual()`, but the subsequent `ActionRead` check is performed unconditionally over `updatedSched`.

This results in an update being rejected even though the user did not modify the backup schedule or its BackupStorage reference.

Interestingly, removing the restricted schedule as part of the same update avoids the check because the loop over `updatedSched` becomes empty.

Expected behavior: An update to unrelated DatabaseCluster fields should not fail solely because an unchanged backup schedule references a BackupStorage that the user cannot read. Authorization should still be enforced when backup schedules or their BackupStorage references are added or modified.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a DatabaseCluster with a backup schedule referencing a BackupStorage named `admin-storage`.

2. Ensure the user has `DatabaseCluster` update permission but does not have `ActionRead` permission on `admin-storage`.

3. Have an administrator attach the backup schedule to the user's DatabaseCluster, or otherwise create this valid state.

4. Update only an unrelated field, for example:
   `spec.engine.replicas: 1 -> 3`

5. Keep the existing backup schedule unchanged in the update request.

6. The handler evaluates `backupSchedulesEqual(oldSched, updatedSched)` as `true`, so the backup schedule creation permission check is skipped.

7. However, the handler then iterates over `updatedSched` and checks `ActionRead` on `admin-storage`.

8. The check fails with `ErrInsufficientPermissions`.

9. The DatabaseCluster update is rejected even though the backup schedule was not modified.

10. As a comparison, submit the same replica update while removing the restricted backup schedule. The `updatedSched` loop is then empty and the update is allowed.

### Relevant Logs / Output

No additional runtime error is required to reproduce this issue.

The API request is rejected with an RBAC `ErrInsufficientPermissions` error for the unchanged BackupStorage referenced by the existing backup schedule.

The important behavior is that `h.next.UpdateDatabaseCluster(ctx, db)` is never reached.

### OpenEverest Version

main branch Commit: 3273653f23ff2e75c840700f772a92a8e8d2f6bc

### Installation Method

Helm

### Kubernetes Distribution

GKE

### Environment Details

OpenEverest commit:
3273653f23ff2e75c840700f772a92a8e8d2f6bc

The behavior was verified from the RBAC handler implementation.

Relevant file:
`internal/server/handlers/rbac/database_cluster.go`

Relevant function:
`UpdateDatabaseCluster()`

### Possible Solution

The BackupStorage `ActionRead` check should be applied based on whether the backup schedule or its BackupStorage reference is being added or modified, rather than re-validating unchanged dependencies on every DatabaseCluster update.

A regression test should cover:

- An existing backup schedule references a BackupStorage inaccessible to the user.
- The schedule remains unchanged.
- The user updates an unrelated DatabaseCluster field.
- The update succeeds.

The test should also verify that adding or modifying a schedule to reference an inaccessible BackupStorage continues to be rejected.

### Additional Context

The relevant control flow is:

`backupSchedulesEqual(oldSched, updatedSched)`
→ unchanged schedules
→ backup creation permission check skipped
→ `for _, sched := range updatedSched`
→ `ActionRead` on BackupStorage
→ `ErrInsufficientPermissions`
→ update rejected

This creates an inconsistent behavior:

- Keeping the restricted schedule + changing replicas: rejected
- Removing the restricted schedule + changing replicas: allowed

The issue affects DatabaseCluster self-service updates when a privileged administrator has attached a BackupStorage that the tenant cannot read.

This appears to be an authorization/update-isolation issue rather than a security vulnerability.

body:
### What is the issue?

In `internal/server/telemetry.go`, if a user misconfigures `TELEMETRY_INTERVAL` to `0s`, `time.ParseDuration` successfully parses it as `0`. 

When the initial metrics delay expires, the background job loop executes `timer.Reset(interval)`. In Go, calling `Reset(0)` causes the timer to fire immediately. Because `collectMetrics()` makes synchronous HTTP requests to the Kubernetes API server and the Telemetry endpoint, this triggers a tight, unthrottled execution loop. 

Instead of waiting, the operator aggressively spams both endpoints as fast as network latency allows, resulting in a self-inflicted Denial of Service (DoS) and spiking the operator's CPU usage. I expected configuration validation to reject zero or negative durations.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Deploy the OpenEverest operator.
2. Edit the operator deployment to set the environment variable `TELEMETRY_INTERVAL=0s`.
3. Wait for the `initialMetricsDelay` (5 minutes) to pass.
4. Observe the operator's CPU usage spike and monitor the excessive `GET` requests hitting the Kubernetes API server (fetching Namespaces and DatabaseClusters).

### Relevant Logs / Output

```go
// internal/server/telemetry.go
interval, err := time.ParseDuration(c.TelemetryInterval)
// ...
timer := time.NewTimer(initialMetricsDelay)
defer timer.Stop()
for {
    select {
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return
    case <-timer.C:
        timer.Reset(interval) // If interval is 0, this timer fires instantly
        err = e.collectMetrics(ctx, *c) // Executes synchronously, returns, and loop repeats instantly
    }
}
```

### OpenEverest Version

Latest (main branch)

### Installation Method

Helm

### Kubernetes Distribution

GKE

### Environment Details

_No response_

### Possible Solution

Add strict validation in `cmd/config/config.go` (`ParseConfig`) to ensure the telemetry interval meets a sane minimum threshold (e.g., at least 1 minute).

```go

interval, err := time.ParseDuration(c.TelemetryInterval)
if err != nil {
    return nil, err
}
if interval < time.Minute {
    return nil, errors.New("TELEMETRY_INTERVAL must be at least 1m")
}
```

### Additional Context

_No response_

title: fix(version_service): bound io.ReadAll response to prevent OOM crash

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Reviewed and accepted; this should be done

body:
### What is the issue?

In `pkg/version_service/client.go`, the Everest server fetches supported 
database engine versions from an external HTTP endpoint and reads the 
entire response body into memory using `io.ReadAll(res.Body)` with no 
size limit enforced.

If the external version service endpoint is compromised, misconfigured, 
or intercepted (e.g. a Man-in-the-Middle attack or a rogue internal 
service), it could return an infinitely large or excessively large HTTP 
response stream. Since `io.ReadAll` dynamically allocates memory until 
EOF with no upper bound, the Everest server will blindly consume all 
available memory until the OS kills the process (`OOMKilled`) or the 
Go runtime panics — causing a complete Denial of Service (DoS).

**What happened:**
The server reads the full HTTP response body with no size cap, making it 
vulnerable to memory exhaustion if the upstream version service returns 
an abnormally large payload.

**What was expected:**
The response body read should be strictly bounded to a safe maximum size 
(e.g. 10MB) using `io.LimitReader`, so that an oversized or malicious 
response fails gracefully with a clear error instead of crashing the 
entire server.

This is a well-known Go security anti-pattern flagged as 
**CWE-400 (Uncontrolled Resource Consumption)**.


### Steps to Reproduce

1. Clone the repository and navigate to the project root:

   git clone https://github.com/openeverest/openeverest.git
   cd openeverest

2. Create a local HTTP server that streams infinite bytes on the
   version service endpoint and run it:

   go run malicious_server.go

3. Point VersionServiceURL to the local server:

   export EVEREST_VERSION_SERVICE_URL=http://localhost:9999

4. Start the Everest server:

   go run ./cmd/main.go

5. Trigger a version fetch:

   curl http://localhost:8080/v1/database-engines

6. Observe Everest process memory spiking until the server crashes
   with an OOM panic or is killed by the OS (OOMKilled).


### Relevant Logs / Output

Detected during manual code review using Antigravity AI security scanner.

The following vulnerable code was flagged in
pkg/version_service/client.go:

   b, err := io.ReadAll(res.Body)

Antigravity flagged this as:

   SEVERITY : High
   CWE      : CWE-400 (Uncontrolled Resource Consumption)
   RULE     : G110 - Potential DoS vulnerability via decompression bomb
   FILE     : pkg/version_service/client.go
   MESSAGE  : Unbounded io.ReadAll on HTTP response body with no size
              limit. A malicious or compromised upstream server can
              stream an infinitely large response causing the process
              to exhaust all available memory (OOMKilled) resulting
              in a complete Denial of Service.

Expected runtime panic if triggered:

   runtime: out of memory: cannot allocate 1140850688-byte block
   fatal error: out of memory

   goroutine 43 [running]:
   io.ReadAll(...)
       /usr/local/go/src/io/io.go:713 +0x105
   github.com/percona/everest/pkg/version_service/client.go:99


### OpenEverest Version

v1.0.0

### Installation Method

CLI (everestctl)

### Kubernetes Distribution

EKS

### Environment Details

_No response_

### Possible Solution

Replace the current unbounded io.ReadAll call in
pkg/version_service/client.go:99 with a size-limited
read using io.LimitReader:

CURRENT (vulnerable):

   b, err := io.ReadAll(res.Body)

FIXED:

   const maxResponseSize = 10 * 1024 * 1024 // 10 MB
   b, err := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(res.Body, maxResponseSize))

WHY THIS WORKS:

   io.LimitReader wraps the response body and stops
   reading after the defined byte limit is reached.
   Even if the upstream server streams infinite bytes,
   the process will never allocate more than 10 MB
   for this response, preventing OOM crashes.

ADDITIONAL HARDENING (recommended):

   1. Set an HTTP client timeout to prevent slow-loris
      style attacks:

      client := &http.Client{
          Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
      }

   2. Check Content-Length header before reading if
      present:

      if res.ContentLength > maxResponseSize {
          return nil, errors.New("response too large")
      }

   3. Make the limit configurable via a constant or
      environment variable so it can be tuned without
      a code change:

      var maxResponseSize = env.GetInt64(
          "VERSION_SERVICE_MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES",
          10*1024*1024,
      )

REFERENCES:

   CWE-400 : Uncontrolled Resource Consumption


### Additional Context

The vulnerable function reads the full HTTP response 
body from the Percona Version Service endpoint without 
any size restriction. Below is the full context of 
the affected code:

FILE: pkg/version_service/client.go

   func (c *Client) getVersions(ctx context.Context) ([]byte, error) {
       req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, c.url, nil)
       if err != nil {
           return nil, err
       }

       res, err := c.http.Do(req)
       if err != nil {
           return nil, err
       }
       defer res.Body.Close()

       // VULNERABLE LINE - no size limit on response body
       b, err := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
       if err != nil {
           return nil, err
       }

       return b, nil
   }

ATTACK SCENARIO:

   1. Attacker performs a Man-in-the-Middle (MITM)
      attack or compromises the upstream version
      service endpoint.

   2. The server returns an infinitely large or
      extremely large response body.

   3. io.ReadAll keeps reading and allocating memory
      until the process is OOMKilled by the OS or
      Kubernetes.

   4. The Everest pod crashes, causing a complete
      Denial of Service for all connected database
      clusters.

IMPACT:

   - Availability: HIGH
   - All database management operations served
     by Everest become

title: fix(cli): reject unknown subcommands on grouping commands
body:
## Why

`everestctl namespaces`, `settings`, `accounts`, `settings rbac` and `settings oidc`
exist only to group subcommands. All five accepted an unrecognised subcommand and
exited `0`, so a typo was indistinguishable from success — silently for three of
them, and with a help dump for the other two. Scripts and CI pipelines that gate on
the exit code could not tell a misspelled invocation from a real run.

Fixes #2816 

## Root cause

Cobra checks `!c.Runnable() → flag.ErrHelp` (`command.go:955`) *before* it validates
`Args` (`command.go:968`). That produced two variants of the same bug:

- `namespaces`, `settings`, `accounts` — `Args: cobra.ExactArgs(1)` plus an empty
  `Run`. The stray subcommand satisfied the arg count, the empty `Run` executed, and
  the process exited `0` with no output at all.
- `settings rbac`, `settings oidc` — `Args: cobra.ExactArgs(1)` and **no** `Run`.
  Being unrunnable, they returned `flag.ErrHelp` before `Args` was ever consulted,
  printed help, and exited `0`.

The consequence is that removing `Args`/`Run` alone does not fix this: a command must
be runnable for its `Args` validator to run at all.

## What changed

Each grouping command now sets `Args: cobra.NoArgs` and a `RunE` that prints help.
`cobra.NoArgs` already emits the exact "unknown command" error we want, so no custom
error construction was needed, and `RunE` makes the command runnable so the validator
is reached.

This matches the convention already used elsewhere in the CLI — `status`, `install`,
`upgrade`, `uninstall` and `version` all use `cobra.NoArgs` and were already correct.

## Behaviour

Before:

```console
$ everestctl namespaces llist
$ echo $?
0
```

After:

```console
$ everestctl namespaces llist
Error: unknown command "llist" for "everestctl namespaces"
Usage:
  everestctl namespaces <command> [flags]
$ echo $?
1
```

Invoked bare, the commands print their help and exit `0`:

```console
$ everestctl namespaces
Manage Everest database namespaces

Usage:
  everestctl namespaces <command> [flags]
$ echo $?
0
```

**One change beyond the reported bug:** bare `everestctl namespaces` previously exited
`1` with `accepts 1 arg(s), received 0`. It now prints help and exits `0`, which is the
conventional behaviour for a command that only groups subcommands, and is consistent
with `everestctl --help`. Flagging it in case reviewers would rather keep the non-zero
exit there.

## Testing

Adds `commands/commands_test.go`, the first test in this package. It drives the real
`rootCmd` and asserts that each grouping command returns an error for an unknown
subcommand, succeeds when invoked bare, and still routes to genuine subcommands.

I confirmed the tests fail against the previous code by reverting `namespaces.go`
(empty `Run`) and `settings/rbac.go` (no `Run`) and re-running — both variants of the
bug are caught.

`make test` passes in full under `-race`. `golangci-lint` reports no issues in
`commands/...`. `make copyright-check` passes; four files picked up the OpenEverest
copyright line via `make copyright-headers`.

`make check` still reports two `misspell` findings in
`internal/server/handlers/rbac/kubernetes_test.go`. These are pre-existing on `main`
and unrelated to this change, so I have left them out to keep this PR to one concern.

title: feat(plugins): implement backend modes (requestHandler, daemon, eventConsumer)

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Reviewed and accepted; this should be done

body:
## Summary

Add `spec.backend.modes` to the `Plugin` CRD and wire it through the controller so the host can actively manage plugin lifecycle: mint daemon tokens, poll health endpoints, and pre-warm event stream slots.

## Background

The [003 generic plugins spec](https://github.com/openeverest/specs/blob/main/specs/003-generic-plugins.md) describes three backend behavioral patterns that the host should understand:

- **Request handler** — the default; proxies HTTP from `/v1/plugins/{name}/*` to the backend.
- **Daemon** — background worker with no inbound user traffic. The host mints a long-lived service token, mounts it as a projected Secret, and polls a `healthPath` to track liveness.
- **Event consumer** — holds an open SSE connection to `/v1/events` and reacts to lifecycle changes.

These are not mutually exclusive; a billing plugin may use all three.

## Why this matters

Today the host treats every plugin as a dumb reverse-proxy target. It has no way to know whether a backend is interactive, a background worker, or an event subscriber. The plugin author must reinvent auth, health checking, and reconnection logic in every plugin.

Some infrastructure already exists:

- `pkg/plugintoken/service.go` — mints RS256 service tokens for daemon-mode plugins.
- `pkg/rbac/plugin_denylist.go` — blocks daemon tokens from writing spec-001 resources.
- `internal/controller/extension/plugin_controller.go` — reconciler with a `// Phase 3+ will add: daemon token minting, NetworkPolicy generation` comment.
- `internal/server/plugins.go` — proxy that routes `/v1/plugins/{name}/*`.

What is missing:

- `PluginBackend` in `api/extensions/v1alpha1/plugin_types.go` has no `Modes` field.
- The generated CRD silently prunes any `spec.backend.modes` block on write.
- The reconciler does not read modes, so it never triggers token minting or health polling.
- `InstalledExtension` status does not surface `TokenIssued` or `BackendReachable` conditions.

## Related

- openeverest/specs#15 — removed modes from the spec doc until this issue is resolved.
- openeverest/generic-plugin-template#7 — removed modes from the template chart.
- openeverest/plugin-audit#10 — removed modes from the audit chart.
- openeverest/openeverest#2803 — reported the CRD pruning bug that prompted the removals.

## Suggested approach

1. Add `PluginBackendModes` struct and `Modes *PluginBackendModes` field to `PluginBackend`.
2. Regenerate CRD with `make generate manifests`.
3. Extend `PluginReconciler` to mint tokens and update `InstalledExtension` conditions when `modes.daemon` is present.
4. Add health polling loop to the reconciler (or a separate controller) that updates `BackendReachable`.
5. Optionally scope the `/v1/events` stream by declared `types` and `namespaces` when `modes.eventConsumer` is present.

Mark as blocked or close once the spec and template charts are restored.

title: CLI parent commands (namespaces, settings, accounts) silently exit with 0 on invalid subcommands

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Reviewed and accepted; this should be done

body:
### What is the issue?

# CLI parent commands (namespaces, settings, accounts) silently exit with 0 on invalid subcommands

## Description

Parent CLI commands that exist solely to group subcommands — such as `everestctl namespaces`, `everestctl settings`, `everestctl accounts`, `everestctl settings rbac`, and `everestctl settings oidc` — are misconfigured with `Args: cobra.ExactArgs(1)` combined with an empty `Run` function. As a result, when a user passes an invalid or misspelled subcommand, Cobra's built-in "unknown command" detection is bypassed, the empty `Run` executes as a silent no-op, and the process exits with status code `0` as if the command succeeded.

This creates a misleading user experience (typos appear to "work" with zero feedback) and is especially dangerous in automation/CI pipelines that check exit codes to detect failures — a misspelled `everestctl` command in a script would silently do nothing and still report success.

## Impact

- Users get no feedback when they mistype a subcommand, making the CLI feel broken or unresponsive.
- CI/CD pipelines and automation scripts that gate on exit codes cannot detect a misconfigured or mistyped `everestctl` invocation, since it returns `0` regardless.
- Increases support burden, as failures caused by typos are indistinguishable from successful runs in logs.

## Affected files

| File | Lines | Command |
|---|---|---|
| `commands/namespaces.go` | ~28-31 | `everestctl namespaces` |
| `commands/settings.go` | ~27-30 | `everestctl settings` |
| `commands/accounts.go` | ~27-30 | `everestctl accounts` |
| `commands/settings/rbac.go` | ~27-30 | `everestctl settings rbac` |
| `commands/settings/oidc.go` | ~27-30 | `everestctl settings oidc` |

Example (`commands/namespaces.go`):
```go
var namespacesCmd = &cobra.Command{
	Use:  "namespaces [flags]",
	Args: cobra.ExactArgs(1),
	Run:  func(_ *cobra.Command, _ []string) {},
}


### Steps to Reproduce

```markdown
1. Build or install `everestctl` from the `main` branch (no cluster connection is required, since the bug occurs before any real command logic executes).
2. Run any parent command with an invalid or misspelled subcommand, for example:
   ```bash
   everestctl namespaces llist
   ```
3. Observe that no output/error is printed, and the command exits as if it succeeded.
4. Check the exit code:
   ```bash
   echo $?
   ```
5. **Result**: Exit code is `0` (success), even though `llist` is not a valid subcommand.

Same behavior can be reproduced with the other affected parent commands:
```bash
everestctl settings unknown-command
echo $?   # prints 0

everestctl accounts something
echo $?   # prints 0

everestctl settings rbac bogus
echo $?   # prints 0

everestctl settings oidc bogus
echo $?   # prints 0
```
```

### Relevant Logs / Output

```markdown
**Actual output:**
```bash
$ everestctl namespaces llist
$ echo $?
0
```
No error message, no help text, no indication that `llist` is invalid — the shell prompt returns immediately with a success exit code.

```bash
$ everestctl settings unknown-command
$ echo $?
0
```

```bash
$ everestctl accounts something
$ echo $?
0
```

**Expected output (for comparison):**
```bash
$ everestctl namespaces llist
Error: unknown command "llist" for "everestctl namespaces"
Run 'everestctl namespaces --help' for usage.
$ echo $?
1
```

There are no crash logs, stack traces, or stderr output associated with this bug — the issue is precisely the *absence* of any output or error signal where one is expected.
```

### OpenEverest Version

v1.0.0

### Installation Method

CLI (everestctl)

### Kubernetes Distribution

EKS

### Environment Details

- Kubernetes Version: v1.28.0
- Host OS: Ubuntu 22.04
- Cloud Provider: AWS (EKS)
- Go version: (as specified in go.mod for the everestctl build)
- Cobra library: spf13/cobra (as vendored in go.sum)

Note: This bug is reproducible independent of the Kubernetes/cluster environment, since it occurs purely at the CLI argument-parsing layer before any cluster connection or API call is made.


### Possible Solution

Remove the empty `Run` function and instead implement `RunE` on the affected parent commands (`commands/namespaces.go`, `commands/settings.go`, `commands/accounts.go`, `commands/settings/rbac.go`, `commands/settings/oidc.go`) so that an unrecognized subcommand returns an explicit error and non-zero exit code, e.g.:

```go
var namespacesCmd = &cobra.Command{
	Use:  "namespaces [flags]",
	Long: "Manage Everest database namespaces",
	RunE: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) error {
		if len(args) > 0 {
			return fmt.Errorf("unknown command %q for %q", args[0], cmd.CommandPath())
		}
		return cmd.Help()
	},
}


Simply deleting Args/Run without this validation is not sufficient — Cobra would just fall back to cmd.Help() via flag.ErrHelp, which still exits 0.

### Additional Context


**Additional Context:**
```markdown
This is a CLI-level bug and does not depend on any particular cluster state, workload, or OpenEverest resource configuration. It affects any user or automation script invoking `everestctl` with a misspelled subcommand under `namespaces`, `settings`, `accounts`, `settings rbac`, or `settings oidc`.

I'd like to work on this fix — happy to submit a PR implementing the `RunE` validation across all affected command files once assigned.

title: Add `everestctl restore delete` subcommand

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Reviewed and accepted; this should be done

body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?

Restores can be created and listed from the terminal but not removed. Restores are imperative history (`restore list` is the audit trail), so records accumulate forever; pruning old or failed entries requires the UI or `kubectl delete`, bypassing Everest API authentication/RBAC.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Add a `restore delete` subcommand. Required flags: `--name`, `--namespace`. Deleting a Restore removes the history record — no stored backup data is touched — so it sits at the resource-removal tier of the shared confirmation pattern (#2658):

- **Interactive:** y/N prompt, default No. Declined exits non-zero without doing anything.
- **`--yes`/`-y`** skips the confirmation.
- **Non-interactive:** if stdin is not a TTY *or* `--json` is set, and `--yes` wasn't given, fail immediately (exit 1) with *"confirmation required in non-interactive mode; re-run with --yes"*.

**In-flight guard:** if `status.state` is `Pending` or `Running`, the command refuses with exit 1 — e.g. *"restore \"my-mongo-restore-x7k2q\" is still running; wait for it to finish or re-run with --force"*. `--force` overrides the guard; when forcing, the confirmation prompt warns that interrupting an in-flight restore triggers the provider's cleanup of the engine restore and can leave the target instance in an inconsistent state. `Error` is deliberately not guarded (deleting a stuck operation is the normal remediation). `--force` is orthogonal to `--yes` — scripted force-deletes need both (`-y --force`), keeping the #2658 rule that `--force` is never a `--yes` synonym. This is a client-side accident guard, not an invariant: it is race-prone by nature and kubectl bypasses it; a server-side guard was deliberately avoided because it would wedge `instance delete --deletion-policy Cascade` on Running children and break GitOps pruning. If the API later enforces this server-side with an override parameter, `--force` maps onto it.

Optional flags:
- `--wait` / `--timeout` — poll until GET returns 404 → exit 0, timeout → exit 124. Ctrl-C cancels only the wait.
- `--ignore-not-found` — same semantics as `instance delete`: already-absent exits 0, short-circuiting prompt and wait.

A 404 is mapped to `restore %q not found in namespace %q`. Follows existing CLI conventions: `--json`/`--verbose`, `--cluster`, `--context`.

### How would users interact with this feature?

```
# Delete a restore record (prompts y/N)
everestctl restore delete --name my-mongo-restore-x7k2q --namespace everest

# Scripted cleanup of finished restores
everestctl restore delete --name my-mongo-restore-x7k2q --namespace everest -y --ignore-not-found

# Abort and delete a restore that is still running
everestctl restore delete --name my-mongo-restore-x7k2q --namespace everest -y --force
```

### Alternative solutions considered

`kubectl delete restore` — bypasses Everest API authentication/RBAC.

### Additional Context

Applies to v2 (`release-2.0`). Reuses the shared confirmation helper and waiter from #2658/#2660. Completes create/list/delete for the `restore` group (#2620, #2621).

title: Add `everestctl backup delete` subcommand

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Reviewed and accepted; this should be done

body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?

Backups can be created and listed from the terminal but not removed — retention housekeeping (pruning old on-demand backups, cleaning up failed ones) still requires the UI or `kubectl delete`, bypassing Everest API authentication/RBAC.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Add a `backup delete` subcommand. Required flags: `--name`, `--namespace`.

What deletion means is governed by the Backup's `spec.deletionPolicy` (`Delete`, the default, removes the engine-native resource **and the artifact in the BackupStorage**; `Retain` removes the resource but leaves the data recoverable out-of-band). The confirmation tier follows the shared pattern established by `instance delete` (#2658) and adapts to the effective policy, which the CLI reads from the Backup before prompting:

- **Policy `Delete` (data loss):** type-the-name confirmation, stating the blast radius first, e.g. *"This permanently deletes backup \"pre-upgrade\" and, per policy Delete, its data in storage \"my-s3\". Type the backup name to confirm."*
- **Policy `Retain` (resource removal):** y/N prompt, default No, noting the data stays in storage.
- **`--yes`/`-y`** skips the confirmation.
- **Non-interactive:** if stdin is not a TTY *or* `--json` is set, and `--yes` wasn't given, fail immediately (exit 1) with *"confirmation required in non-interactive mode; re-run with --yes"*.

**In-flight guard:** if `status.state` is `Pending` or `Running`, the command refuses with exit 1 — e.g. *"backup \"nightly\" is still running; wait for it to finish or re-run with --force"*. `--force` overrides the guard. `Error` is deliberately not guarded (deleting a stuck operation is the normal remediation), and `Deleting` needs no guard. `--force` is orthogonal to `--yes` — scripted force-deletes need both (`-y --force`), keeping the #2658 rule that `--force` is never a `--yes` synonym. This is a client-side accident guard, not an invariant: it is race-prone by nature and kubectl bypasses it; a server-side guard was deliberately avoided because it would wedge `instance delete --deletion-policy Cascade` on Running children and break GitOps pruning. If the API later enforces this server-side with an override parameter, `--force` maps onto it.

No policy-override flag at delete time: `spec.deletionPolicy` is mutable on a live Backup, so changing the artifact's fate is an update, not a delete option (and the field freezes once deletion starts, so an override could race).

Optional flags:
- `--wait` / `--timeout` — block until the Backup is actually gone (provider cleanup of engine resources/artifacts runs behind a finalizer): poll until GET returns 404 → exit 0, timeout → exit 124 with a message that cleanup is still running server-side. Ctrl-C cancels only the wait.
- `--ignore-not-found` — same semantics as `instance delete`: already-absent exits 0, short-circuiting prompt and wait.

A 404 is mapped to `backup %q not found in namespace %q`. Follows existing CLI conventions: `--json`/`--verbose`, `--cluster`, `--context`.

### How would users interact with this feature?

```
# Delete a backup (policy Delete → states blast radius, asks to type the name)
everestctl backup delete --name pre-upgrade --namespace everest

# Scripted retention pruning
everestctl backup delete --name nightly-20260701 --namespace everest -y --ignore-not-found

# Abort and delete a backup that is still running
everestctl backup delete --name hung-backup --namespace everest -y --force

# Wait until the artifact cleanup finished
everestctl backup delete --name pre-upgrade --namespace everest -y --wait --timeout 10m
```

### Alternative solutions considered

`kubectl delete backup` — bypasses Everest API authentication/RBAC.

### Additional Context

Applies to v2 (`release-2.0`). Reuses the shared confirmation helper (`pkg/cli/confirm`, both tiers) and the shared waiter's until-404 condition from `instance delete` (#2658) / `backupstorage delete` (#2660). Completes create/list/delete for the `backup` group.

title: Plugin CRD prunes spec.backend.modes, so plugin-audit's chart declares modes that never reach the API

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Not reviewed by a maintainer yet — not ready to be worked on

body:
### What is the issue?

`plugin-audit`'s Helm chart declares `spec.backend.modes` on its `Plugin` CR, but `PluginSpec` in `api/extensions/v1alpha1/plugin_types.go` has no `modes` field. The CRD generated from it allows exactly three properties under `spec.backend`: `credentialsSecretRef`, `externalUrl`, `serviceRef`. The schema is structural and sets no `x-kubernetes-preserve-unknown-fields`, so the API server prunes the block on write.

The result is that a plugin can declare `requestHandler`, `daemon` and `eventConsumer` in its chart, `helm install` reports success, and none of it reaches etcd. Nothing warns.

I found this while reading the framework to work out what a plugin can rely on, so I checked it rather than assuming. I have not run this against a live cluster; the reproduction below runs the API server's own pruning code offline.

### Steps to Reproduce

Reproduces from clean clones with Go and Helm, no cluster needed.

1. Render the chart and confirm `modes` is really emitted:

```
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/openeverest/plugin-audit.git
helm template audit plugin-audit/charts/audit/ | grep -A6 'modes:'
```

2. Run the shipped CRD and that rendered CR through `k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apiserver/schema/pruning`, which is what the API server calls on write. Full program: https://gist.github.com/LarytheLord/c19caf1a52d2e3f93c0f731bff265026

Or check the schema directly, which shows the same thing:

```
git clone --depth 1 --branch release-2.0 https://github.com/openeverest/openeverest.git
grep -n 'modes' openeverest/config/crd/bases/extensions.openeverest.io_plugins.yaml   # no match
```

3. On a cluster the equivalent check is `helm install` the audit chart, then `kubectl get plugin audit -o yaml` and look for `spec.backend.modes`.

### Relevant Logs / Output

Output of the pruning program against `release-2.0` at `eefde0e`:

```
CRD: plugins.extensions.openeverest.io (group extensions.openeverest.io)
PreserveUnknownFields (spec-level): false
served version: v1alpha1

=== fields the apiserver DROPS on write ===
  DROPPED: spec.backend.modes

=== spec.backend as it would be STORED ===
serviceRef:
  name: audit
  namespace: default
  port: 8080
```

What the chart asks for, from `helm template`:

```yaml
  backend:
    serviceRef:
      namespace: default
      name: audit
      port: 8080
    modes:
      requestHandler:
        basePath: "/"
      daemon:
        healthPath: "/healthz"
      eventConsumer:
        types:
          - database-cluster.created
          ... 23 event types total
```

`config/crd/bases/extensions.openeverest.io_plugins.yaml` is the only Plugin CRD in the org (not in `helm-charts`, not in `openeverest-operator`), and `dev/Tiltfile:220-221` applies it with `kustomize('config/crd')` while the Helm release uses `skip_crds=True`, so this is the schema that is actually served.

### OpenEverest Version

release-2.0 @ eefde0ef225cceea19fc85565fe03e211825c86c

### Installation Method

Manifests / Manual

### Kubernetes Distribution

Other (please specify below)

### Environment Details

No cluster. The reproduction runs the apiserver's structural-schema pruning offline against the CRD in the repo and the chart-rendered CR.

Go 1.26.3, Helm v4.1.3, k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver v0.31.3.

### Possible Solution

Depends which side is meant to be right, and I do not know that.

If `modes` is intended, adding it to `PluginSpec` and regenerating the CRD makes the chart work as written. `plugin-audit`'s backend does not currently depend on it: `getToken` in `backend/internal/consumer/consumer.go` authenticates as a service user against `POST /v1/session`, and `pkg/plugintoken.Mint` has no callers in this repo, so daemon mode looks designed but not wired up yet.

If it is not intended yet, removing the block from the chart would stop it advertising something that does not take effect.

Either way a validating webhook or an admission warning on unknown `spec.backend` keys would turn this from silent into visible, since pruning gives the chart author no feedback at all.

### Additional Context

Related but filed separately if wanted: the `plugin-audit` README documents `EVEREST_TOKEN_PATH=/var/run/secrets/everest/token` as a mounted plugin service token, while the code uses the service-user login above. The two disagree about how a plugin gets its own identity.

title: fix: remove incorrect IncreaseTimeout call from DeleteSession
body:
The DeleteSession (logout) function was calling attemptsStore.IncreaseTimeout(ip). The problem is that this function is supposed to be used only when someone fails to log in, because it increases the penalty time for that IP. But here, it was being triggered even on logout, which is actually a successful action.

Because of this, every time someone logged out, the timeout for their IP kept doubling, which made it harder and harder for them to log back in later. In short, logout was wrongly treated like a failed login attempt, and that ended up blocking legit users from logging in again.
